items.title: 11.4.4 Graph of y = tan x from -pi to pi

source_refs.note: Book p. 209-210: 11.4.4 Graph of y = tan x: behaviour near +/-pi/2 cases (i)-(iv) (ii)-(iv) misprinted, table 0 to pi, graph -360 to 360 with asymptotes, properties (i)-(viii).

blocks.text: We know that \(\tan(-x) = -\tan x\) and \(\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x\), so the values of \(\tan x\) for \(x = 0^{\circ}, 30^{\circ}, 60^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}\) can help us in making the table.
Also, we know that \(\tan x\) is undefined at \(x = \pm 90^{\circ}\), when

items: (i) \(x\) approaches \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) from left, \(x \to \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{-}\), \(\tan x\) increases indefinitely in Quard I.
(ii) \(x\) approaches \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) from right, i.e., \(x \to \left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{+}\), \(\tan x\) increases indefinitely in Quard IV.
(iii) \(x\) approaches \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) from left, i.e., \(x \to \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{-}\), \(\tan x\) increases indefinitely in Quard II.
(iv) \(x\) approaches \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) from right, i.e., \(x \to \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{+}\), \(\tan x\) increases indefinitely in Quard III.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book's cases (ii) to (iv) give wrong directions or quadrants (and spell Quadrant as 'Quard'). Correct:
(ii) just right of \(90^{\circ}\) (e.g. \(91^{\circ}\)) the angle is in Quadrant II, not IV, and \(\tan x\) decreases indefinitely: \(\tan x \to -\infty\).
(iii) just left of \(-90^{\circ}\) (e.g. \(-91^{\circ}\), the same as \(269^{\circ}\)) the angle is in Quadrant III, not II; \(\tan x \to +\infty\) is right.
(iv) just right of \(-90^{\circ}\) (e.g. \(-89^{\circ}\)) the angle is in Quadrant IV, not III, and \(\tan x\) decreases indefinitely: \(\tan x \to -\infty\).
Case (i) is correct: Quadrant I, \(\tan x \to +\infty\). The book's own table (\(90^{\circ} + 0\) gives \(-\infty\)) and its graph agree with these corrections.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does this happen? \(\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Near \(\pm 90^{\circ}\), \(\sin x\) is close to \(\pm 1\) while \(\cos x\) is close to \(0\); dividing by a very small number gives a very large answer. The sign of the answer is the sign of tangent in that quadrant:
\(89^{\circ}\) (Quadrant I): \(\tan 89^{\circ} \approx 57.3\), large positive.
\(91^{\circ}\) (Quadrant II): \(\tan 91^{\circ} \approx -57.3\), large negative.
\(-91^{\circ}\) (Quadrant III): \(\tan(-91^{\circ}) \approx 57.3\), large positive.
\(-89^{\circ}\) (Quadrant IV): \(\tan(-89^{\circ}) \approx -57.3\), large negative.
We know that the period of tangent is \(\pi\), so we shall first draw the graph for the interval from \(0\) to \(\pi\) (from \(0^{\circ}\) to \(180^{\circ}\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(90^{\circ} - 0\) means 'a little less than \(90^{\circ}\)' and \(90^{\circ} + 0\) means 'a little more than \(90^{\circ}\)'. \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) are not numbers you can plot; they say that the curve shoots up (or comes up from far below) close to \(90^{\circ}\). The vertical line \(x = 90^{\circ}\), which the curve approaches but never touches, is called an asymptote and is drawn dashed. The values after \(90^{\circ}\) come from \(\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x\): \(\tan 120^{\circ} = -\tan 60^{\circ} = -1.73\).
Since the period of \(\tan x\) is \(\pi\), we have the following graph of \(y = \tan x\) from \(-360^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = tan x from -360 to 360 degrees. The x-axis is marked every 90 degrees with radian names, the y-axis from -4 to 4. Dashed vertical asymptotes at x = -270, -90, 90 and 270 degrees. Between each pair of neighbouring asymptotes one increasing branch comes up from far below, crosses the x-axis at -180, 0 or 180 degrees and rises steeply upward; the outer half-branches start at (-360, 0) and end at (360, 0). Table points at 0, 30, 60, 120, 150 and 180 degrees are marked.
blocks.caption: Graph of y = tan x from −360° to 360°, asymptotes dashed (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The heading says 'from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\)'; the book's figure shows more, \(-360^{\circ}\) to \(360^{\circ}\). The part from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\) is the middle of the figure: one full branch between \(-90^{\circ}\) and \(90^{\circ}\), plus a half branch on each side. Because the period is \(\pi\), every branch is a copy of the branch through the origin moved by a multiple of \(180^{\circ}\). Each branch rises from left to right: tangent increases on every interval between two asymptotes.
Properties of graph of tangent function (y = tan x)

items: (i) The domain is the set of real numbers except the values where function is undefined: domain of \(\tan x = (-\infty, \infty)\), \(x \ne (2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(ii) The range includes all real numbers \((-\infty, \infty)\).
(iii) The graph of \(\tan x\) is not continuous for all real numbers. It breaks at \(x = (2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(iv) The period of tan function is \(\pi\). Mathematically, we can express it as \(\tan(\theta + \pi) = \tan\theta\).
(v) The tan function is an odd function, as the graph of tan function is symmetric about the origin. Mathematically, it can be written as \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\).
(vi) The \(x\)-intercept of the tangent function occurs at \(x = \pi n\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
(vii) The \(y\)-intercept of the tangent function is \(0\).
(viii) The amplitude of tangent function is undefined because it has no maximum or minimum values.

blocks.caption: The three graphs compared (our summary of the properties in 11.4.2 to 11.4.4)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: In a sketch of \(y = \tan x\) always draw the asymptotes \(x = \pm 90^{\circ}, \pm 270^{\circ}\) as dashed lines first, then the branches. The curve must come very close to these lines but never cross or touch them.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Period \(\pi\): one branch between two asymptotes, repeated every \(180^{\circ}\).
2. Asymptotes (breaks) at \(x = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}\), where \(\tan x\) is undefined.
3. Range: all real numbers; no maximum, no minimum, no amplitude.
4. Zeros at \(n\pi\); the graph passes through the origin; odd function.
5. Left of an asymptote \(\tan x \to +\infty\); right of it \(\tan x \to -\infty\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Joining the branches across an asymptote: the graph has a break there.
2. Writing the period of tangent as \(2\pi\) (that is sine and cosine).
3. Writing \(\tan 90^{\circ} = \infty\) as a value: \(\tan 90^{\circ}\) is undefined.
4. Copying the book's cases (ii) to (iv): just right of \(90^{\circ}\) and just right of \(-90^{\circ}\), \(\tan x\) goes to \(-\infty\).
